newsitem.title: USA: AT&T set to revise Worldnet Internet pricing.
newsitem.headline: AT&T set to revise Worldnet Internet pricing.

text.p: AT&T Corp plans to unveil Wednesday a new pricing plan for its WorldNet Internet service, changes analysts speculated will complete its move to the flat rate industry standard of $19.95 a month.

In addition, analysts believe the telecommunications giant is likely to extend its current offer of five free hours of Internet acccess per month to customers of its long-distance phone services, a bid to hold the line on customer turnover.
AT&T's current pricing options call for WorldNet Internet access service customers who do not subscribe to AT&T long distance services to pay a flat rate of $24.95 per month.
Current AT&T phone customers already qualify for a flat rate plan that charges $19.95 per month.
A spokesman for the telecommunications giant declined to comment on the nature of the pricing changes to be announced, saying only that service pricing is "always under evaluation."

"The world has turned to flat rate pricing at $19.95 except for AT&T," Forester Research new media analyst Kate Delhagen said. "(AT&T is) either going to chop that rate back and make it competive or extend the free hours offer indefintely," she predicted.
Nine months ago when it introduced its WorldNet consumer Internet access service, WorldNet was one of the pioneers in introducing a flat-rate monthly pricing option on its service.
But industry changes spurred in part by AT&T's entry into the business have led many rivals to respond with flat rate plans of their own that run $19.95 a month.
The AT&T spokesman said that since its introduction in March, AT&T WorldNet service has signed up 500,000 customers, making it one of the nation's largest direct Internet access providers.

Noting that the free five hour offer was due to expire at the end of December, Peter Krasilovsky, an Internet industry analyst with Arlen Communications Inc, said, "This gives (AT&T) an excellent opportunity to start charging for their service."
On the other hand analysts don't expect AT&T to try and undercut current pricing for Internet services.
"The (profit) margin on this $19.95 all-you-can-eat offer is so thin already," Delhagen said.
"AT&T is not in the habit of offering their services for less than others...so don't expect to see any more free pricing coming out of that company," Krasiolovsky agreed.
